meta.title: Stellar Apps: software execution platform for AI in space
meta.authorsHtml: Arnau Prat<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Armin Purle-Kopacz<sup>1</sup>, Hendrik Otte<sup>1</sup>, Daniel Lüdtke<sup>1</sup>

meta.venue: Proceedings of the 3rd Conference on AI in and for Space (SPAICE 2026)

abstract: The increased complexity of space missions, coupled with emerging trends such as long-duration missions and large satellite constellations, demands new approaches to autonomy and on-board data handling. Artificial Intelligence (AI), and in particular Machine Learning (ML), is a key enabler of on-board autonomy and data processing in space systems. However, deploying AI applications on-board spacecraft poses significant challenges in terms of safety, cybersecurity, and resource usage constraints, to name a few. This paper presents Stellar Apps, a software platform designed to enable the safe and secure execution of untrusted third-party applications, including AI-based ones, on spacecraft computers. Stellar Apps provides isolation, multi-tenancy, real-time support, and access to AI accelerators, while enabling incremental in-orbit updates. In this paper, we discuss how Stellar Apps facilitates the execution of AI applications in space.

blocks.html: Space technology is undergoing a paradigm shift characterized by shorter development cycles, cost-efficient missions, and an increasing number of commercial and institutional actors. At the same time, missions are becoming more ambitious, involving long-duration operations, large constellations and a higher degree of autonomy. Traditional spacecraft software architectures, which are usually static, mission-specific and tightly coupled to hardware, struggle to meet these new demands.

Artificial intelligence offers promising solutions for on-board autonomy, data processing, and health management, among others. By processing data directly on board, known as edge computing, spacecraft can reduce downlink requirements, react faster to events, and operate more independent from the ground. However, integrating AI and ML into spacecraft systems introduces new challenges, including trustworthiness, safety certification, cybersecurity, and human-AI interaction.

In particular, the main challenges of bringing AI applications on board are related to resource constraints, security, and software infrastructure. Space systems operate under strict limitations in terms of computing power, memory, and energy. At the same time, AI models can exhibit nondeterministic behaviour and often rely on complex software dependencies, which raises concerns about security and the need to properly isolate them from mission-critical software. In addition, running these models requires an appropriate software stack that is typically not available in traditional spacecraft systems.

These challenges highlight the need for the development of AI platforms capable of ensuring the safe and secure execution of third-party applications using potentially untrusted AI libraries under resource constraint environments. To address this need, the Stellar Apps platform [1] is under development aiming to provide a standardized, secure, and flexible execution of applications, similar in concept to an "app store" for spacecraft.

Recent developments in spacecraft flight software increasingly favour modular and application-centric platforms that enable flexibility, reuse, and in-orbit updates. Frameworks such as ESA’s NanoSat MO Framework (NMF) demonstrates the feasibility of deploying and managing on board apps, including AI-based applications [2]. Open source initiatives like KubOS further explore the idea of extensible on-board platforms for small satellites [3]. More recent research investigates container-like execution modules and differential updates to support evolving on board functionality [4]. Within this landscape, Stellar Apps advances the state-of-the-art by combining strong application isolation, multi-tenant execution, real-time support, cybersecurity, and native AI acceleration into a unified platform specifically designed for safe ML-based applications.

Recent work also shows that Artificial Intelligence is increasingly being integrated into space systems to support on board autonomy and decision-making under resource constraints. As an example, federated learning frameworks have been proposed to enable distributed model training across LEO constellations with limited communication and computing resources, highlighting the feasibility of efficient on-board learning across satellites [5]. Deep learning has also been applied for real-time image classification on board satellites, as shown by data-centric competitions like the OPS-SAT on-board classification challenge [6].

Autonomous control and reinforcement learning approaches are being explored to advance trusted satellite operations and high-level decision making, demonstrating safe inference in simulated and isolated environments [7]. There are reviews of AI accelerators at the hardware and inference layer that show how neural network inference can be enabled under harsh space conditions while balancing computational efficiency and radiation tolerance [8]. These developments reflect a state-of-the-art where on-board AI supports data processing, autonomy, and resilience, moving beyond traditional ground-centric workflows and exploiting edge computing in future missions.

In this paper we present Stellar Apps as the future goto execution platform for AI applications in space. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 presents the Stellar Apps platform. Section 3 describes the AI approach of Stellar Apps. Section 4 presents use cases and applications. Finally, Section 5 gives the conclusions and an outlook to future work.

Stellar Apps is a software platform under development at the German Aerospace Center (DLR) that enables the secure, efficient, and flexible use of on-board computing resources by multiple applications, including third-party and AI-based ones. With Stellar Apps, third-party applications and system services can be deployed as self-contained on-board applications in a safe and secure way. Configurable access controls ensure safe interaction with spacecraft systems and computing resources. This architecture allows operators to continuously evolve spacecraft capabilities by adding, updating, or replacing apps as mission needs change. The ability to securely run and validate complex software reduces risks and significantly speeds up the time from idea to orbit.

The platform is designed to support the safe and efficient execution of modern AI and high-performance computing tasks on board spacecraft. This requires a combination of strong application isolation and cybersecurity, support for modern AI software stacks, efficient access to hardware accelerators, and mechanisms for secure updates and multitenant operations throughout the mission life-cycle. The main requirements for the platform are:
• Application isolation: each application runs in a separated environment with configurable access to spacecraft data and hardware, ensuring mission safety.
• Incremental updates: applications can be updated or replaced during the mission, supporting multi-mission spacecraft and evolving requirements.
• Development environment parity: developers can use an environment similar to the on-board execution context, reducing integration risks.
• AI-enabled: support for common frameworks such as PyTorch and Tensorflow, as well as access to AI accelerators and hardware platforms like the Nvidia Jetson.

A prototype of Stellar Apps has been developed to validate design decisions and conduct experiments. Figure 1 shows a screenshot of the prototype being used with the NASA Operational Simulator for Small Satellites (NOS3).

blocks.html: Three virtual machines (VM) are used to simulate the different segments that Stellar Apps provides software for: user, ground, and space (Figure 2). Each of these virtual machines holds a registry to store applications at different development stages. Communication between these virtual machines is realized by TCP/IP connections. The NOS3 simulator visualizes the spacecraft and simulates its position. The application orchestrator uses this position to schedule applications.

Each AI application is encapsulated as a container image and orchestrated via Podman atop a Linux environment. System isolation is achieved through the utilization of kernel namespaces, while control groups (cgroups) are employed to enforce strict resource quotas on CPU, memory, and I/O utilization; this ensures that anomalous application behavior does not result in resource exhaustion for other system components. Real-time deterministic behavior is guaranteed by the underlying real-time kernel in conjunction with the Stellar Apps runtime. Hardware acceleration is abstracted through a set of APIs that interface directly with Stellar Apps services. To ensure system integrity, all applications are digitally signed and verified prior to deployment, with subsequent maintenance handled via incremental updates. The current prototype is validated across four hardware platforms: the PolarFire SoC (RISC- V), Xilinx Zynq (ARM), Nvidia Jetson and LEON5 (for the different system services).

The Stellar Apps approach for AI is centered on enabling safe, efficient, and flexible deployment of machine learning applications directly on board the spacecraft. Rather than embedding AI tightly into mission-specific flight software, Stellar Apps treats AI algorithms as isolated applications that run within a controlled execution environment. This decoupling allows AI models to be developed, tested, updated, and replaced independently of the core software, significantly reducing integration risks and life-cycle costs. The platform provides access to commonly used AI frameworks as well as to hardware accelerators, while enforcing strict resource management and interface-based access. By combining application isolation, real-time execution support, and secure APIs, Stellar Apps enables the use of AI for a wide range of tasks and applications.

A development kit is provided to application developers. It is designed to closely resemble the deployment environment, thereby minimizing discrepancies between development, testing, and operational executions. This environment enables developers to begin creating application iterations early on under realistic system conditions.

The development kit includes a standardized Application Programming Interface (API) that serves as the primary communication interface between applications and the platform. This ensures consistent integration patterns and promotes interoperability across the ecosystem. The kit is accompanied by complete documentation, including an installation guide, ground interface instruction manual, getting-started guide, and detailed API documentation, as shown in the Figure 3.

Stellar Apps enables the developers to do rapid prototyping and to develop AI applications in an agile way. Apps that are deployed to the spacecraft can be improved iteratively by using incremental updates. As mentioned previously, isolating the application on board protect the spacecraft from critical software bugs that can occur during development. Applications can be deployed to space early and AI models can be improved and adopted to new conditions. Testing services of a dedicated ground interface (see Figure 4) can enable validation under representative hardware and system conditions prior to deployment.

blocks.html: Access to specific on-board software modules or hardware subsystems requires appropriate entitlements. These are granted by the operators of the ground interface, based on mission requirements and risk assessment. Given the potential impact on spacecraft safety and mission integrity, entitlement allocation is subject to strict review and procedures.

Entitlements also govern applications that do not only process data but influence spacecraft behaviour. Commanding of critical on-board subsystems is possible, but requires a dedicated entitlement, granted only after a dedicated risk assessment. This does not affect isolation since applications never access subsystems directly, but exclusively through the platform’s dedicated interfaces. Additionally, this access is supervised a the data broker between applications.

Overall, this framework established a structured yet accessible development pathway, enabling developers to design, test, validate, and mature their applications in a controlled environment, and to transition them seamlessly from early development stages to operational deployment in orbit.

An additional key advantage of the proposed framework is the simplified access to on-board hardware accelerators. AI acceleration is enabled through hardware such as NVIDIA Jetson GPUs and FPGA-based AI accelerators. Through abstraction of the hardware interface layer, applications can transparently leverage AI acceleration resources available within the system. By decoupling application logic from low-level hardware, the framework exposes standardized interfaces that allow developer to utilize this capabilities without requiring detailed knowledge of the underlying hardware architecture. This abstraction significantly reduces development complexity, improves portability across different hardware configurations, and enables efficient execution of computationally intensive workloads.

By abstracting spacecraft-specific interfaces and communication layers, Stellar Apps removes the need for developers to handle low-level space protocols, proprietary middleware, or mission-specific software frameworks. Applications interact with spacecraft resources exclusively through standardized and well-documented APIs, rather than directly accessing complex communication stacks or hardware drivers. This approach eliminates the requirement for detailed knowledge of space system internals and allows developers to work in an environment comparable to a conventional Linux-based system. As a result, development effort is reduced, portability is improved, and AI specialists without prior space background can contribute applications without compromising safety or system integrity.

Stellar Apps enables a wide range of on-board AI and edge computing applications including autonomous health management for satellite constellations, sensor data preprocessing to reduce downlink volume, on-board scientific data analysis, digital twins running on-board to predict system behavior, real-time earth observation processing such as wildfires or optical navigation for on board servicing among many others.

Within the scope of the Stellar Apps project conducted at DLR, a series of on-board applications are developed and progressively validated for in-orbit operation over the coming years. In addition, use cases from industry partners and others such as high performance signal processing are being considered and integrated.

Several of these applications make extensive use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) techniques. The following three applications exemplify the AI-centric capabilities enabled by the platform.

ATHMoS [9]: ATHMoS aims to detect anomalies and novel patterns in satellite telemetry and to autonomously inform ground engineers of significant deviations from nominal system behaviour. To achieve this, ATHMoS continuously constructs and updates a model of the satellite’s recent nominal operational state directly on board. Using this adaptive model, selected telemetry parameters are monitored and processed in near real time to identify statistically or semantically novel behaviour. Upon detecting a relevant anomaly, the system triggers a notification to ground operators via the messaging service provided by ODARIS. By performing novelty detection on board, ATHMoS reduces reliance on continuous ground-based monitoring and enables faster response times to potential critical events.

ODARIS [10]: ODARIS provides a unified on-board information management layer that enables low-latency access to satellite data at any time. Its primary objectives include real-time system parameter monitoring, structured data access, and instantaneous alarm generation. Beyond its role as an information backbone, ODARIS provides services that can be leveraged by AI-driven application such as data provisioning, event handling, and communication interfaces to ground system. In the context of AI-enabled operations, ODARIS serves as both a data source and a dissemination channel for on board inference results, and thereby supporting autonomous as well as semi-autonomous mission concepts.

Satellite Attitude Estimation and Tracking [11]: This application addresses the problem of pose estimation for cooperative or uncooperative satellites operating in close proximity to a robotic service spacecraft. The application processes three-dimension sensor data such as point clouds generated by on board LIDAR systems to compute accurate and real-time estimates of the satellite relative pose. The system combines deep learning-based pose initialization module with a classical model-base tracking algorithm to achieve both robustness and precision. The estimated pose information is provided to the robotic and Guidance, Navigation and Control (GNC) subsystem to support missioncritical operations such as target identification, final approach, and capture. This hybrid AI-classical approach demonstrates how advanced perception algorithms can be integrated into safety-critical space robotics applications.

In this paper, we presented the Stellar Apps platform as an enabler for onboard artificial intelligence in future space missions. The increasing autonomy, complexity, and operational lifetime of modern spacecraft require a shift from static, mission-specific flight software towards modular, evolvable, and application-centric architectures. Stellar Apps addresses this need by providing a secure and standardized platform for the deployment and management of on-board applications, including third-party and AI-based software.

By combining strong application isolation, multi-tenant, real-time capabilities, secure update mechanisms, native support for AI frameworks, and the use of more powerful on-board computers and hardware accelerators; Stellar Apps overcomes many of the limitations of traditional spacecraft software architectures and challenges with bringing AI to space. The platform decouples AI functionality from core flight software, enabling incremental validation, controlled access to spacecraft resources, and reduced integration risks. This architectural approach allows AI applications to be developed, tested, verified, and updated independently, thereby significantly shortening development cycles as well as increasing mission flexibility.

The presented proof-of-concept illustrates the technical feasibility of the approach at architectural level. In particular, the integration of containerization, standardized APIs, hardware abstraction, and accelerator access provides a practical pathway for deploying computationally demanding AI models directly on board. A quantitative evaluation of the platform has not yet been carried out and is the focus of ongoing work. This future evaluation will cover application upload, installation, run-time overhead, robustness of the platform and the performance of AI accelerators.

In the long term, Stellar Apps aims to foster a sustainable and collaborative European space application ecosystem by defining lightweight, open and extensible interfaces. By enabling industry, academia, and agencies to develop, validate, and deploy on-board applications within a common framework, the platform can serve as a foundation for an "app-enabled" spacecraft paradigm. As a generalpurpose platform, Stellar Apps does not itself constraint the application domain.

As space systems continue to evolve towards higher autonomy and on-board intelligence, platforms such as Stellar Apps will play a central role in unlocking the full potential of artificial intelligence and machine learning in orbit by transforming spacecraft from static systems into continuously evolving, software-defined elements.
